text:
You come up out of nothing the way a diver breaks the surface — no shore behind it, no swim you remember taking. One moment there is no you at all. Then there is: flat on your back on a floor that is cool and close-carpeted, a ceiling above you doing a competent impression of a ceiling.

You take inventory the only way you trust it, which is from the outside in. Your breath is going fast — you clock that before you clock being afraid, and read the fear off the breath rather than the other way round. Your hands are pressed flat to the carpet, holding on, as though the floor were a thing that might quit. Heartbeat loud under your own ribs. Nothing hurts. For one blank second you don't have your own name, and then you do — *Alan* — and it arrives clean and sure and fastened to absolutely nothing else. No door you came through. No before.

Then the letters.

They assemble in the air a foot off your face, pale and frameless, a pane the frost-color of a cold window, text writing itself across it in a hand that is not a hand. It does not ask. Something passes over you — through you — a cool flat attention laid down your whole length like a tailor's tape, and the pane fills as it reads.

{{system}}

It gives you back to yourself in a column of quiet facts, and you find you can read them untaught — where you are strong, where you are thin. Low on the pane, one line where a value should sit stays blank. Not zero, not hidden behind anything — the line simply has nothing in it. Set apart from the rest, two facts that are not about you: the name of the place — the Harem Hotel — and its floor, and the floor is the first.

Then the attention lifts off you. The pane holds another moment, indifferent as a receipt, and goes still.

You sit up into a hallway.

It runs long both ways, and it is expensively long — the corridor of a place that spent money to make you feel you had arrived somewhere. Close one way, not far, the hall ends at a wide door standing a hand's-width open on a room plainly meant for you: a bed built for more than one, low warm light, a made and waiting place. The other way the hall runs on, and narrows, and darkens toward a single shut door at the very end — and you understand without deciding to which end is the soft one and which is not.

You are still testing whether your legs intend to cooperate when the soft end of the hall does a thing walls do not do. The wall beside the open door seams without a sound and *grows* — a second doorway pressing itself out of flat plaster, molding and lintel and all, as if the corridor had recalled it wanted one more room here and simply put one in.

A woman comes out of it.

She stops in the doorway itself — one hand laid flat to the molding the wall has only just finished making, testing that it holds — and looks at you a while before she says anything, as though the looking were the part worth doing slowly.

You take her the way you took the pane — fast, off the edges first. Tall. Dressed for somewhere warmer than a basement: deep sapphire silk off the one shoulder, a thread of silver at her wrist. Silver-white hair. A scatter of pale scales high on each cheekbone catching the low light, and two dark horns swept back off her brow that your mind reaches to file under *costume* and can't. Her eyes are a pale silver-grey, round-pupiled, and already on you — have been, you would guess, a beat longer than yours have been on her.

"There you are," she says. She takes in the whole picture of you — landed on the floor of your own hallway, read but not yet risen — and her smile does not widen so much as settle in, unhurried, like someone who already knows how the evening goes and is glad of it anyway. "The first thing you do is lie there and read yourself before you will trust your own feet." A held beat. "That is a better opening than most manage on purpose."

"First off, you are stunningly beautiful," you say, up at her from the floor. "Second: do you know where we are? I can't seem to remember how I got here."

The words leave you and hang in the warm hall light. She does not reach to deflect them or perform modesty over them; she lets the compliment sit out in the open, received; a gift half-expected and welcome all the same.

"Stunning," she repeats, and keeps the word, turning it over once. "You've no idea where you are or how you came to be here — and you led with that." The beat she leaves is warm, and longer than it needs to be. "I think I'm going to enjoy you. That was fast work."

She comes off the doorframe, crosses to you, and folds down onto the carpet an arm's length away, silk pooling around her. She looks entirely at home on the floor of a hallway, a woman who has held conversations in worse spots than this.

"Where we are." She turns the question over the way she turned the compliment, and for once the answer doesn't come easy. "I don't have it. Truly. I came into this place much the way you seem to have — elsewhere one moment, here the next, no door behind me I can point to — and it hasn't seen fit to explain itself to me any more than it has to you." A glance up the long dim reach of the hall toward the far shut door, then back to you. "Whatever your pane told you when it measured you is very likely the sum of what either of us holds. Two people at the bottom of a thing neither can name past its name. I'd rather hand you that straight than play at being your map."

"And the how of it I have even less, if that's possible — only that my own blank matches yours. You woke with the front of your life torn off; I can't tell you what tore it, or whether this place does that to everyone it takes or did it to just the two of us." Her eyes come back to yours and hold. "But you are not doing this alone — that part I can make true just by staying. And I have always found the not-knowing to be the good part. So we'll call it that, and start there."

She puts out a hand — not to haul you up, only offered, palm open across the small distance of floor between you.

Your hand closes on hers — the grip of someone making sure the one solid thing in the room stays where it is — and you pull. She gives you her weight to brace against and rises as you rise, until you are both standing, close, closer than the leverage strictly needed, and you have not let go of her hand.

Her fingers settle in around yours rather than slipping loose, and they stay there — the hold yours to keep for as long as it does you any good.

"Up you come." She looks you over once you are standing. "On your feet, in your own hall. Better."

"Okay." You are on your feet now, her hand still in yours. "Where do we go from here?"

She turns her head to answer it with her eyes first; you follow the look. The hall runs its two directions off the small warm patch of floor the two of you make. Close on one side: the open door, the made bed, the low easy light. The far side darkens down its length to that single shut door at the end, patient, waiting on nobody.

"Two doors." A tilt of her head — first at the near one, then down the dark. "I don't know this place any better than you do, so take it as a reader's guess and not gospel: that near one — open, warm, already made up — has the look of somewhere to rest. And the far one, shut, all the way down there in the dark, has the look of somewhere that wants something from you before it opens." Her thumb moves once across the back of your hand, there and gone. "If I had to call it: the near way is the kinder one, and the far way is the adventure. But I'm guessing at a room I've not been inside. We could find out slowly — there's no clock on us that I can hear."

"What do you suppose that shut door wants of me?" You say it half to her, half to the dark down the hall — thinking aloud more than asking.

She doesn't answer right away.

Your thumb moves over the back of her hand — the same slow stroke she gave you a moment ago, returned — and her hand turns a fraction in yours, pressing back into the hold: the ball come back over the net. Then the corner of her mouth deepens, and the look she gives you holds more frank interest than it did a breath ago.

"Now that," she says, "is exactly the right question — and I don't have the answer to it. That's the honest place to start." She holds a beat, unhurried. "And here's the truer thing: even if this place leaned down and whispered what waits behind that door, I don't think I'd pass it to you. Tell a man what's coming and he spends the whole walk bracing for the thing you named — and misses what's actually there. I wouldn't want to take that from you."

Then her gaze drops from yours for a moment and comes back, and she leans the smallest degree closer. "I'll give you one thing anyway, because I find that I want to — and hear me say it plain: I've no right to promise this. But whatever that door asks of you, I think you'll meet it. I've known you the length of one hallway, and I already believe it."

"I guess I need to explore the open door, then." You are already turning, drawing her gently by the hand toward it. "Would you come with me?"

She comes. That is the answer, ahead of any more words: she moves with it, her weight going easy, matching your step down the short soft-lit stretch of hall.

"The open door it is." A beat, two, her hand loose and willing in yours. "I did say the adventure was the other way. I notice you're taking me the interesting direction regardless."

The door stands open on the room that was waiting for you, and you cross into it — and the strangeness of the place lands on you sideways: it is furnished like somewhere you already live. The bed is made, and made to your taste. The light sits where you would have set it. A chair stands angled to a reading-lamp, put exactly where your hand would reach for it — the placement of someone who had watched you read a hundred evenings, except no one has, and there were no hundred evenings, and you have never once stood in this room.

Behind you, without a sound, the door eases itself shut on the hall.

And the pane comes back.

Smaller than the first — a single cornered rectangle in the same frost-color, text writing itself into the air at the edge of your sight in the same lettering as before, that no hand seems to shape:

{{system}}

Nothing else. No why, no toward-what. It states the thing the way the first pane stated your name — flat, incurious — and holds, and does not explain itself. Behind you she has gone quiet; you cannot tell yet whether she can see it too.

"Did you get a message just now?" You turn to her — she is just inside the shut door, where you drew her. "I just got a... a quest. To close the distance between us."

She looks where you're looking — you watch her do it — to the patch of air a foot off your face where the letters hang for you. Her eyes track across it and catch on nothing.

"I got no message." You watch her face wake right up — and she does not step back. "So it talks to you, and not to me," she says, quiet, working it as she goes. "And the very first thing it wants —"

"...is for us to get closer." You finish it for her — and then you give her the rest of it, her hand still warm in yours. "What do you want to do?"

She's quiet a moment. You watch her weigh it — not the question, you think, but the thing behind it she can't see.

"Three thousand years I've decided when the scene gets warm," she says at last, low. "And now there's something in the air by your face I can't read, telling us to." Her mouth crooks. "I don't take its notes. It doesn't get to call this one."

A beat. Her hand tightens around yours, once, and eases.

"But I won't dress this up: I find I want to anyway — and that's mine, not its." She leaves the last of the distance exactly where it is, uncrossed, the smallest gap held open between you. "So. Your hand, and your call." Her eyes stay on yours. "Do you want to come the rest of the way — or shall I?"

You step into her, and the last of the distance closes to nothing — the gap she held open gone, the whole length of her against you, silk and the give of her under your hands, your joined grip caught folded at your chests. "I've never wanted anything more."

Your hands hold her without a tremor — your pulse gone slow and sure where you'd have guessed it would race.

You feel the small hitch of her breath — caught, for a beat, on yours.

"Say it to me again, just like that," she says, low — the plainest you have heard her. "Exactly that plain. I don't want the better version. I want the one you just gave me."

Her free hand comes up to your jaw — light, just resting there — and she stops, that close, her breath at your mouth.

You close the gap once again, all the way this time, and kiss her, slow — no rush anywhere in it. Her mouth is warm and yields under yours, and for a moment there is nothing but that: the soft press, the deepening by degrees, her lower lip caught light between yours and let go.

She makes a low sound into it — just the sound of her — and her hand slides up into your hair, curling at the back of your neck to hold you close. She takes it at the tempo you give her.

Slow, and slower — you draw it long — until it eases apart on its own, your mouths parting a bare inch, her forehead tipping to rest against yours.

For a moment neither of you moves — her forehead against yours, the made room gone quiet around you, the shut door and the whole strange place forgotten on the far side of it. You can feel her breath on your mouth, still coming a little uneven from the kiss, and the small unwillingness in her to be the first to draw back. So you are not the first either. You stay exactly there, in the last of it.

Then, past her shoulder, the pale letters come. The same frost-color, the same flat hand, as indifferent to the moment as it was to your name in the dark:

{{system}}

{{system}}

{{system}}

No ceremony to it — it states what you crossed and what the crossing paid you, the way a ledger states a sum, and goes quiet. You let the letters go. She is warm against you, real in a way the pane will never be, and nothing it could tally is worth the turn of your head from that.

She feels the shift in your attention anyway — not to the letters, which she cannot see, but the half-second your focus goes past her and comes back. Her mouth curves against your jaw.

"It's talking to you again," she says. Not a question. "I can always tell. You go somewhere for a beat, and then you come back deciding something." She draws her head off yours, just far enough to find your eyes. "Decide it, then."

"I already did." Your voice comes out lower than you mean it to. "Back in the hallway. I just hadn't caught up to myself yet."

You watch it reach her — the small pause before she decides what to do with it — and what she does is tip her mouth back up to yours, and this time she is not matching your pace. She is setting it. The kiss goes deep and slow and deliberate, and her hands come off your chest and slide up under the open front of your shirt, palms flat, dragging the fabric back off your shoulders as she goes.

"Here is where I stop being polite about it," she says against your mouth, the words gone thick at the edges. "I have wanted my hands on you since I stepped out of a wall that opened where none had been. I have been very patient. I do not intend to be a moment longer." She gets the shirt down your arms and off, and drops it without looking where it falls. "I mean to take my time with you. Do try to keep up."

"That sounds like a warning."

"It is a promise. They're better." Her palms spread across your bare chest, and she takes a breath at the feel of you under them, small and real, there and gone. "The wanting still surprises me. Every time. As if I hadn't done this before." Her eyes come up. "I hadn't. Not once. Not this."

You want to ask her what she means — this, as opposed to what — but her hands are moving and her mouth is at your throat and the question loses to the answer of her. You get your own hands on her at last: the warm give of her waist through the silk, the long line of her back, the place where the sapphire gown is fastened at her shoulder. You find the fastening by feel and work it loose.

The silk goes off her shoulder, and then, when she shrugs once to help it, off her entirely — and it pools at her feet and she stands for it, unhurried, while your eyes go where they will. You had thought you knew what she looked like. You did not. The scatter of silver at her cheekbones runs further than the gown ever let on — a bright faint tracery that comes down the side of her throat, over her collarbone, spreads in a fine web across one shoulder and down along the inside of her arm to the wrist. It catches at the small of her back, low, where your palm settles, and it is warmest there, or feels warmest under your hand. Her skin everywhere is warm and smooth and human enough to undo you and not quite human at all, and the not-quite is the part you cannot stop looking at.

The dark horns catch the lamplight when she turns her head to watch you look. She does not cover anything, does not shift her weight to hide or to pose. She gives you the whole of her to look at, and her face is doing something frank and unguarded and pleased — pleased clean through, to be seen like this, to be wanted this plainly by a man who is not bothering to hide that he is staring.

"You look like the pane did," she says softly. "When it read you. Like you're taking inventory." Her mouth crooks. "Take it. I'll wait. There isn't a piece of me I'd hide from you tonight."

"I don't have words for most of it."

"Then don't use any." She reaches out and takes your wrist and draws your hand up, off the small of her back, and sets your palm flat over the silver web on her shoulder, pressing it there. "Tell me the way you just did in the hall. With your hands, and nothing dressed up." Her voice drops. "I have heard every pretty speech there is, and made most of them. I would trade the lot for the plain thing you keep doing."

So you do it plainly. You trace the silver where it runs — down her throat, along her collarbone, out across her shoulder — and you feel her breath change under your hand where it goes, quicker at her throat, caught when you reach the soft skin inside her wrist. You bring your mouth down to follow your fingers, and when you set your lips to the line of silver at her throat she makes a low sound, more air than voice, and her hand comes up into your hair to hold you there.

She walks you back toward the bed that was made to your taste, and the backs of your knees find the edge of it, and she puts one hand flat to your chest and pushes, once, and you go down onto it. Then she comes down over you — deliberate, taking her time — and settles her weight full against you, and for a while there is only the give of her and her mouth working unhurried down your throat.

Her mouth goes down your chest, your stomach, lower, and closes warm around your cock, and she takes her time with it exactly the way she promised — the flat wet heat of her mouth, her tongue, one hand wrapped at the base of you and the other spread on your hip to keep you where she wants you. She is unhurried and she is thorough and she is plainly, wholly enjoying herself, and she tells you so with every sound she makes around you. You get a hand into her silver hair — not to move her, just to hold some part of her — and she hums at that, low, and the hum goes all the way up your spine.

When it starts to be too much, when your hips want to move and she can feel it, she draws off you and looks up at you with her mouth wet and her eyes bright and absolutely unrepentant.

"Not like that," she says. "Not the first time. The first time I want all of you, and I want to be looking at your face when I take it." She comes back up over you, one long slow drag of her whole body against yours, and settles astride your hips, and you feel the wet heat of her right where you are hardest. "And I intend to take it very, very slowly, so do not," she leans down and sets her teeth light at your jaw, "hurry me."

She reaches between you and takes you in her hand and guides you to her, and sinks down — slow, an inch, and stops, and breathes, and takes another inch, until she has taken all of you and you are seated as deep in the slick heat of her as you can go. Her head goes back. The tracery of silver on her throat stands out in the lamplight. For a moment she does not move, just holds you there, full of you, her weight settled and her hands flat on your chest.

"There you are," she breathes — the words she met you with, that first hour, before either of you knew what the other was. She says them like she is only now finding out she meant them. She rolls her hips once, a long deliberate figure, and you feel it everywhere. "I have decided when the scene begins and how warm it gets and when it ends, for longer than you would believe. Do you know the one thing that was never mine?" Another roll, slower, drawing a sound out of you that you don't try to hold back. "This. Someone I wanted to slow down for. Something I did not want to be finished with." Her fingers curl against your chest. "So I am going to be greedy, and I am going to take my time, and you are going to let me."

"Slower, then," you manage. "You said slower."

Her laugh comes out cracked at the edges. "Now you're learning."

She rides you slow — the long deliberate rhythm she has made of everything else since the hallway, the rhythm that has been driving you quietly out of your mind all night, now with the whole of her wrapped hot around you. You meet her for it, your hands moving over her — the flare of her hips, the weight of her breasts, the soft skin of her stomach, the place where you are joined slick between you — and every place you touch, she leans into, greedy, wanting more of your hands not less. You watch the control go out of her by degrees. First the rhythm, which starts to catch and stutter. Then her voice, the wit in it thinning out until what is left is just sound, just breath, just your name coming apart in her mouth. Then her face, the composed knowing amusement she has worn since she stepped out of the wall going loose and open and undefended.

"The thing you said in the hall," she says, ragged, her forehead dropping toward yours. "Do you still want it, now that you have it?"

"More," you tell her. "Now that I have it — more, not less." You get a hand into her hair and hold her there, close, your hips meeting hers. "Any of it. All night. I wanted it before I had the shape of it, and I want it more now that I do."

And somewhere in the long middle of it, moving with her, holding her open face a few inches from yours, the thing you did not expect happens.

She goes still over you.

Not that she stops — her hips keep their slow deep rhythm, the pleasure still climbing in both of you toward the same place. But something in her lets go. The knowing, the management, the part of her that has run every moment of this since the hallway with a practiced hand — it drops away, caught and held on a single drawn breath, and for once she leaves her face alone. She just shows it to you. The wanting, and the disbelief underneath the wanting, and under that something older and more tired and more bare than either, that she does not try to hide.

"Keep it exactly this true," she says. "Whatever I make of it after — and I will, I always do — don't let me. Just this. Just what it actually was, and not the lovelier thing I turn it into." Her hips falter and drive deep. "Three thousand years, and I have never once wanted to be held to the true version. Keep it. Keep me to it."

"I'll keep it," you tell her, and you mean it the way you meant the thing in the hall, and she hears that you mean it — you watch her hear it — and it is that, more than your hands or your hips or the whole slow climb of it, that takes her over.

She comes with you buried deep in her, clenching around you, her whole body drawing tight and then breaking open, and she says your name and then nothing, no words, just the sound of her coming undone with her forehead pressed to yours. And the feel of her going over the edge takes you with her, slow and complete, emptying you into her, the two of you holding on through the long shaking end of it until you both just lie there, spent, joined, breathing the same air.

Afterward she stays exactly where she is, still astride you, her weight loose and easy over you, her face tucked into the side of your neck. You can feel her heart going, fast and then slower, against your chest. Neither of you says anything for a long time. Her fingers move idly at your shoulder, tracing something, and you realize after a while that it is the same line of silver she has, drawn on you where you do not have it — mapping her own markings onto your bare skin, as if checking whether they took.

And in the dark past her bare shoulder, the letters come one last time.

The thing that has read TALENT: UNKNOWN since your first hour in this place — the blank line low on the pane, the one value the frost-hand would not fill — is naming itself now. In the same flat indifferent letters that weighed your soul in the dark and gave you back a column of quiet facts, it puts a choice in front of you. And then it stops, and does not go on without you.

And then you feel Aria go rigid against your chest — and it is not your stillness she is matching.

Her head comes up off your neck, sharp. Her eyes fix on a point in the air a hand's breadth from her own face and track across it, catching, the way yours catch on the pane a foot past your own. You know that look from the inside; you have worn it since your first hour here. And you watched her wear the opposite of it once, in the hallway — staring at the empty air where your letters hung and finding nothing there at all. *I got no message,* she said then. *So it talks to you, and not to me.*

It is talking to her now.

"There's —" Her throat moves; for the first time since the hallway she is looking at something she has nothing ready to say to. "There are letters. By my face. Pale ones, and no hand making them." Her eyes move, reading, and whatever it says, she does not smooth it — she gives it to you plain, the way she asked you to keep her. "It never spoke to me before. Not once, in all my years. And now it wants me to choose something." She turns her gaze off the pane and back to you, and there is something raw and wondering in it, and under that the start of a fear she has not named. "It wants me to give you a piece of me. And to take a piece of you in return." Her hand finds your jaw, warm. "And tonight, with you still inside me, it finally has something for us both."

You are still inside her, still wrapped in the warmth and the after of it, when the two of you become — for the first time — two people reading the air at once.

She watches her letters; you watch yours. Hers hang where she can see them and you cannot; yours where you can and she cannot. For a moment it is almost absurd, the pair of you gone still and careful over each other's shoulders at nothing the other can find — and you feel the small tremor in her chest of a laugh she does not quite spend.

"Well," she says, low, her voice not yet all the way back to steady. "It seems we are both being asked to be generous." Her eyes track her pane, and her face keeps snagging on it — the wonder, and under the wonder that unnamed edge. "It paid me no mind before now. I have lived a long, long time, and I do not know the first thing about being wanted by it." Then the old warmth finds its way back into her mouth, even here. "You've had longer at this than I have. Go on — show me how it is done."

So you look at your own.

It is not reading you now. It is holding something open, the way a door holds open, and waiting on you to answer. You have had a single night of her, and already you could name a dozen things about her you would not give back — the way she reads a room down to its floor, the way she takes the tempo of a thing in her hand and slows it until it aches, the plain unarguable force of her that bends a night around itself without seeming to ask for it.

You turn your attention full to the pane, and see what it wants of you.

text:
You look at what the pane is holding open, and you already know the answer — you have known it since the hallway, maybe, without the word for it.

Of everything she is, you could take her read on a room, or the tempo she keeps in her two hands — the slowing that has undone you all night. But neither has held you longest. It is the plain force of her: the fact of the whole strange night bending itself around her without her seeming to ask it to. That. You reach for it, and you tell the pane so.

She is watching your face while you do it. She cannot see your letters, but she can read the moment you decide — she told you so, in the dark, not an hour ago. Then her own pane pulls her eyes back to itself, and it is her turn.

You watch her read it. Whatever it lays in front of her, she takes her time with, as she does with everything; and then her gaze lifts off the letters and settles on you, and there is something careful in it, something already choosing.

"I know what I want of you," she says. Low, and sure. "Not the cleverness — I have cleverness of my own, and yours would only crowd mine." Her thumb moves at your jaw. "The other thing. The part of you that held its ground in the hallway and handed me the plain truth, warm, and did not dress it up or take it back when I gave you every opening to. The part that keeps a thing true when it would be easier not to." Her mouth softens. "That. Weave a little of that into me. God knows I could stand to carry some."

She says it to you and to the letters at once, and you feel — not see, feel — the answer take.

{{system}}

For a moment nothing in the room has changed. Her weight is still loose over you, the lamp still low, the silver still bright along her throat. And under all of it now, a thread — you could not say where it runs or how, only that it is there, drawn taut and live between the two of you, and that when you turn your attention along it you can feel the far end of it living in her.

She feels it too. Whatever moves through her, she lets it reach her face and stay there — she does not reshape it into something lovelier, though you can see the old habit want to. "That is going to take some getting used to," she says, unsteady.

Then, past her shoulder, in the dark at the far end of the made room, the letters change — not the ledger-hand now, but something hung like a direction, pale words pointed toward the door you have not opened. The far one. The shut door at the dark end of the hall that has, from the beginning, looked as though it wanted something of you before it would open.

{{system}}

She feels the turn of your attention toward the dark end of the hall, and this time she asks you nothing — only follows your look, and gathers herself. She lifts off you at last and takes up the sapphire silk from the floor, drawing it closed at her shoulder; and by the time it is fastened the loose ease has gone out of her and left the attentiveness underneath, the alertness she wore in the hallway before any of this began. "So. The night gave us this much." The thread; you feel her mean it. "Let us go and see what the morning means to charge for it." And she is moving before you are, down the hall toward the door you have not opened, one hand held back for yours.

quest.title: FLOOR 1
quest.objective: open the door at the dark end of the hall

text:
The warm end of the hall gives way behind you as you go down toward the cold one — past your own door, past the room the wall grew Aria, to where the light thins and the runners end and the corridor narrows to the shut door it has always narrowed to. It has hung there dark since you woke. Aria comes with you, close at your shoulder, and neither of you pretends this is anything but what it is: the far end, and the thing the far end was built to make you earn.

The door is only a door. You put your hand to it and it swings, silent, as it was always going to, and the cold behind it breathes out over both of you. Whatever the Hotel means to test here, it was never the door.

The chamber beyond is bare and pale and colder than the hall, and it is not empty. The Doorward stands up out of the far wall as you cross the sill — the same dead-white plaster the whole place is grown from, pulling itself whole and upright, a heavy blank body a head taller than you and built wide — and it does not wait to be looked at. It turns toward the two of you with the slow certainty of a thing with one job and the mass to do it. And you came through the door to meet it as you are: one man, empty-handed, nothing on you but the clothes you woke in.

Aria steps up level with you — the Hotel that fits a room to its guest has fitted her to your measure tonight, and she carries it like she has decided not to mind. Her eyes go over the construct, fast and honest. "Slow off the wall," she says, low, "but it'll hit like the wall it came out of." A flick of her chin at the pale chest, where the plaster closed over itself and left a low seam. "And there — that's where it shut itself. Might be soft. I can't tell you for certain from here." Then, plainer, for you: "We're the same size as each other now, you and I. Stay off its inside, keep it between us, and we wear it down."

The Doorward takes its first heavy step, and the cold room narrows to the space between you and it.

text:
"I'll pull it off you," you tell her — "you've got the claws for it, aim for the seam." There is no time to hear whether the plan is good; it is the only one, and a body that size will not wait on your doubts. You break straight for the Doorward, loud and wide open, making yourself the one thing in the room worth turning toward.

It turns for you — slow off the wall, exactly as she said, but the arm that swings round with it is not slow, a whole pale slab of a limb thrown flat at where your head is. You are already not there. You drop back out of its reach on the balls of your feet, the blow shearing the air a hand from your face, close enough to feel the wind of it. That is the gamble: that you are quick where it is strong, that the trick is to be worth hitting and never be where the hit lands.

You give ground and keep giving it, circling, and the construct comes after the insult of you — dragging itself around after the target that keeps sliding off its inside, its back coming round, its blind flank opening to the room. Once its reach closes on the space where you just stood, and you feel exactly how that would have gone had it found an arm to close on. But it closes on nothing. You are three steps gone, and Aria has the opening you bought her.

She takes it without a word. She goes in low and fast at its chest, its attention snarled on you, and her claws find the low seam where it had sealed itself — and this time there is no might-be about it. It gives. Where the warded mass turned everything aside, the seam opens under her hand, and a long crack runs up from it with a sound like a flagstone splitting. The Doorward lurches.

But it is a big thing, and one crack will not bring it down. It wrenches itself off its back foot, the blank head swinging round to find the two of you again — slower now, favoring the cracked side, but up, and still square between you and the door it keeps.

text:
You take its door for your ally. The thing will not leave the doorway — cannot; guarding it is all it's for — so you make the door the ground you fight on, circling tight to its front, staying loud in its blank face, keeping yourself the nearer danger and Aria the one it has no attention to spare for.

You work it as before, pulling its front around after you, meaning to bare the split flank to her again.

But it does not come around. The thing has kept the one lesson the last pass taught it — it holds the cracked side turned inward, hunched toward the wall, and gives Aria the flat of its warded shoulder instead, guarding the door and the wound along the same dull line.

Aria goes for the seam anyway, fast and low where it opened before — and there is nothing there to open. Her claws rake across warded plaster and skid off the hard mass with no purchase under them; she pulls the strike and drops back out of reach a beat before the heavy arm comes round for her. No crack this time. "It's got wise to that," she says, landing back at your shoulder.

The Doorward draws its bulk in square between you and the door, the cracked side kept to the wall, and holds there — not lunging now, not giving, watching the both of you for whatever you mean to try next.

text:
You break the circle the other way. You have gone one way around it long enough for the thing to learn the turn, so you plant and cut back hard against your own line — and for an instant its pivot is committed wrong, leaning after where you were, the guarded side swinging open as it hauls to bring the wall back to it.

You do not give it the beat it needs. You go straight in, inside the reach you have kept clear of till now, and drive the heel of your hand into the seam before it can turn the crack back to the wall. You are no claws — it is not the blow Aria lands — but the crack takes it, splits a shade wider under your weight, and the cold pours out of it against your wrist.

And you are far too close now. The arm you baited comes down for you — you feel it start before you see it — and you throw yourself clear, rolling under it as it cracks into the floor where you stood. You come up out of the roll, the seam open behind you, and Aria is already moving.

She hits it clean — into the crack you tore wide, low and hard, and this time it is her claws in the soft of it. The seam gives all the way, a second split forking off the first, and the Doorward buckles at the middle and rocks back a full step, its heels scraping over the sill of the door it guards.

text:
The thing is still fighting its own weight, heels scrabbling off the lost sill for a floor to set on. You do not let it find one. You are inside its guard before it can, everything you have thrown high — your shoulder into the cracked chest, driving up and back to take it down with you. And it goes: its footing tears away and you crash down together, your slight weight and its far greater one, in a tangle on the cold floor.

But a thing this size does not go down alone. As you drive it over its arms come around you — not fast, but vast, already closing before you can roll clear — and they clamp you to the pale mass as you land, pinning one arm to your side, crushing the air out of you. The pain is white and immediate. You are inside its reach now, with no way back out, and the grip is only tightening.

And Aria is there, reading the ruin of it in the half-second she has — you caught, the seam split wide and turned up to her by the fall. "Hold still," she says, and her hand goes past your cheek, so close it stirs your hair, into the open seam a hand's breadth from where you are pinned. You hold still, and trust the aim.

Her claws go into the crack to the knuckle and tear, and the Doorward answers it — a deep grinding shudder runs through it, the split running wider, something structural giving behind the plaster. The arms around you spasm. And the grip loosens: the crushing weight eases back a fraction, slack for the first time since it closed, as the thing convulses around its wound.

text:
"Don't stop," you tell her — the words forced out against the plaster crushing your chest. Pinned as you are, one arm still caught in its grip, you drive down with everything left to you: your shoulder, your free hand, all your slight weight bearing the cracked mass low, holding its blank attention on you and off the woman at its flank. And it stays down. Above you Aria does not stop — her hand works the split in a sustained tearing, claws in the crack to the wrist, widening it past anything the plaster can draw shut, until the wound opens all the way to its center, to the hard pale core it was all poured around: the keystone, bared at last.

And there is something in it — where the crack runs deepest, half-swallowed in the core, a hard edge catches the light in a way plaster never would: worked metal, a haft, a blade seated in the keystone as though the hall had set it there and grown the guard up around it. The free hand you are bearing down with is a span away. You do not think; you close your fingers on the haft and work it loose — a knife, slim and plain and cold, no longer than your hand.

You know what the knife is for, as surely as you have known nothing else in this place. It is the one thing left you can do, and you do it — you turn it in your fist and drive it back into the keystone it came out of, all your weight behind the one true placement — not power, you have none, but the blade finds the fault and goes home. And the Doorward stops. The grinding, the shudder, the vast grip on your arm — gone, cut clean, the straining mass gone still around you. You lie in the sudden quiet inside dead plaster, the knife buried to its hilt, and it does not move again.

Then the plaster begins to move — not toward you but away, the white mass loosening and drawing back into the wall it grew from, until there is nothing on the floor but you and the knife and Aria. And the floor itself takes a breath — a long slow lift through the soles and the spine, the light along the walls sliding a shade warmer as the whole floor climbs. When it settles the cold chamber is gone, folded away behind you, and the hall runs on ahead — longer, and darker at its far end, where a new shut door has grown where the wall had run unbroken before.

And Aria is a half-step changed. Nothing you could point to, nothing so plain as taller — but she straightens up out of the wreck of the fight more easily than she should, standing into the space a shade more solidly than she had this morning, steadier on the follow-through. As if, in climbing, you had loosed something in her that had been held tight, and the same step that lifted you had lifted some part of her too. You see it take — there, and marked, and set aside. "You went into a wall with your bare hands," she says, turning the little blade a slow look, "and came out holding the one edged thing it was hiding. I could not have written you a better opening." She puts out a hand and pulls you up onto the floor that is not the one you started on.

text:
It is stranger than the fight, the quiet that comes after. You stand on the new floor with the knife still in your hand and the wall sealed smooth where a door of dead plaster had been, and the tiredness hits you all at once. "We should stop," you say. The words come out rough. "Both of us. That was — we need a break after that." Aria does not argue. She looks at you a moment, the knowing brightness of her banked low for once, and inclines her head.

But first you look. You have learned this floor's older sibling well enough to know the shape of the place — the hall running to its dark far end, and nearer, where you stand, the doors of rooms. You try them. This is the lived-in end: a suite that is somehow yours, made up as though it had been waiting on you, and past it a smaller room lit silver-grey that must be hers. You go through both as a man goes through his pockets one more time, thorough and without much hope. A bed, a basin, a lamp, linens folded by hands you never saw. Nothing with an edge to it, nothing that answers to weapon or key. The floor keeps its useful things behind its doors, you are starting to see, and pays them out only to those who get through — and here at the top of the climb there is only the ordinary furniture of rest.

So you set the knife on the table by the bed, where the morning will find it, and you let the day come to its end. Whatever the fight took out of you, the rest gives back; you feel it as you lie down, the deep ache going quiet by degrees, the body remembering how to be whole, the floor holding you like solid ground under a man who has finally stopped falling. Aria is there in the low light, near, the warmth of her a fixed point in a place with none of its own. Neither of you reaches for more than this tonight; the fight is too close behind, and the rest of it can keep. But the two of you went into a wall of moving plaster together and came out the other side, and the thread that runs between you lies a little nearer the surface than it did this morning, close enough to feel if you turn toward it. "Sleep," she says, in the old low voice, the one that turns a plain word into a whole hand laid flat on your chest. "The dungeon will still be there in the morning. It is very good at waiting." And at the dark end of the hall, the new door waits with it.

quests.title: The Far Door
quests.objective: reach the shut door at the dark end of the second floor

bonds.name: Aria
bonds.note: +1 PRESENCE from her — grows as hers grows.

text:
You come up out of sleep all at once and whole, as you have not woken since this place took you — no ache, no ghost of the fight in your shoulder. The lamp has burned down to nothing. Aria is a warm weight along your side, awake, watching you surface with the small pleased look of a thing gone as she would have written it. You roll into her, over her, your mouth finding the line of her jaw. "Fuck for luck," you say against her skin, "before the next door?"

She laughs low in her throat, the sound of it moving through you where you are pressed against her. "Luck," she says, tasting the word as if deciding whether to let you have it. Her hand comes up into your hair, taking its time. "I have no luck to give you, you know. It is not a thing I deal in — no one does; the dice fall where they fall, and I would be lying if I told you my hands could tip them. But this, I will take gladly, and for its own sake, and not because it buys you anything at that door. Come here."

And you do. It is not the careful, astonished thing the first night was; you know each other now, the map of it, what she likes and how she likes to be made to wait for it. She sets the pace — slow where she wants you slow, her mouth curved against yours all the while like she is telling you a story and this is only the part before the good part. You lose the door. You lose the floor and the dungeon and the whole climbing weight of the place; there is only the full weight of her over you, the low sounds she does not trouble to hide, the give and grip of her, and her voice still at your ear — "more patience than that; we have all morning" — until neither of you has patience left for anything, and the morning takes you both.

After, you lie in the tangle of the linens, the risen light grey and plain across the room, the two of you gone loose and quiet. She is the first to move — of course she is. She rises and gathers herself back into the shape the day wants, silver and composed, only the smallest disorder left in her hair to admit the morning happened at all. She hands you your shirt. "No luckier than you were," she says, "but better company for the walk." You could not have looked at the far end of the hall last night without something in you flinching from it. This morning, you find you can. You dress. You take up the knife. You go to see what the second floor has grown to stop you.
